text: When should documentation take place during the troubleshooting process?

options.text: Only once the fault has been fixed
Throughout the entire process, not just at the end
Only if the fault cannot be solved
Before starting work only

explanation: Documentation needs to happen throughout the process, not just at the end. It is one of the most important and most overlooked parts of troubleshooting.

options.text: A visual diagram showing how components connect
A written record of each fault as it happens, capturing key details about the symptom and solution
A software tool that automatically detects faults
A backup of the system taken before work begins

explanation: A fault log is a written record of each fault as it happens. A basic fault log captures the fault number, date and time, symptom, solution, how it was tested, and the technician's name.

text: What are the six fields captured in a basic fault log?

options.text: Fault No., Date & Time, Fault Symptom, Solution, Testing, Technician
User, Device, Error Code, Fix, Cost, Manager
Date, Location, Hardware, Software, Duration, Resolution
Ticket No., Priority, Category, Fix, Time Taken, Approved By

explanation: A basic fault log captures: Fault No., Date & Time, Fault Symptom, Solution applied, how it was Tested, and the Technician's name.

text: What is a fault logging database?

options.text: A single paper sheet used to record one fault at a time
A searchable database of all recorded faults and fixes that grows more valuable over time
A backup system that stores copies of repaired files
A manufacturer's online support portal

explanation: A fault logging database is a searchable collection of all recorded faults and fixes. Over time it becomes extremely valuable for spotting recurring problems and speeding up future repairs.

text: How does a fault logging database become more valuable over time?

options.text: It automatically updates itself with manufacturer fixes
It accumulates records that help spot recurring problems and speed up future repairs
It replaces the need for technicians over time
It connects directly to diagnostic tools

explanation: As more faults are recorded, the database becomes invaluable for spotting patterns, recurring issues, and speeding up future repairs by providing a reference for similar past faults.

text: Where do troubleshooting guides typically come from?

options.text: They are automatically generated by diagnostic software
They are built up from experience and fault log data over time
They are only produced by hardware manufacturers
They are created before any faults have been seen

explanation: Troubleshooting guides are documents built up from experience, often created from fault log data over time. They walk through how to fix known faults step by step.

text: Why is documentation critical when multiple technicians work on the same system?

options.text: It is a legal requirement in most countries
Without it a technician would have no starting point and would need to trace everything from scratch
It speeds up the hardware replacement process
It replaces the need for a fault log database

explanation: Without documentation, even an experienced technician on an unfamiliar system has no starting point and would need to trace everything from scratch.

text: What does the best documentation include beyond just recording what went wrong?

options.text: The cost of replacement parts used
How the system works and how components interact
The user's login credentials
A list of all software licences on the system

explanation: The best documentation explains how the system works and how components interact — not just what went wrong. This gives future technicians the context they need.

text: What are the three types of documentation covered in this module?

options.text: Flowcharts, Handbooks, Internet Resources
Fault Logs, Fault Logging Database, Troubleshooting Guides
Backups, Replacements, Systematic Approach
Linear Notes, Half-Split Records, Test Results

explanation: The three types of documentation covered are: Fault Logs (minimum requirement), Fault Logging Database (scales with the organisation), and Troubleshooting Guides (built from experience).

text: A technician fixes a monitor issue by reconnecting a loose cable. What is the minimum they should record in the fault log?

options.text: Nothing — the fix was too simple to log
Fault number, date and time, symptom (no display), solution (reconnect cable), how tested (display working), and their name
Just the date and the solution applied
The user's name and which software was affected

explanation: Even simple fixes should be fully logged. A basic fault log captures: fault number, date and time, fault symptom, solution applied, how it was tested, and the technician's name.

text: What is the badge that summarises the minimum documentation requirement?

options.text: Scales with the organisation
Built from experience
Minimum requirement
Verify before you start

explanation: 'Minimum requirement' is the badge for Fault Logs — the basic written record every fault should have. The database 'scales with the organisation' and guides are 'built from experience'.

text: Match each documentation type to its correct description.

columnB.text: Step-by-step fix instructions built up from experience and past fault data
A written record of each individual fault capturing symptom, solution, testing and technician
A searchable collection of all recorded faults that grows more valuable over time

explanation: Fault Log = individual record per fault. Fault Logging Database = searchable collection of all faults. Troubleshooting Guide = step-by-step instructions built from experience.
